one_liner: Protected dataplane OS that runs TCP/IP and one app on dedicated polling cores; 2.8-3.6x memcached throughput over Linux+epoll.
what_it_does: IX splits the OS into a Linux control plane (cp/ixcp.py plus the Dune kernel module) and per-application dataplanes. The dp/ix binary runs in VT-x non-root ring 0, owns whole Intel NICs and dedicated hyperthreads, and hosts a single multithreaded application in ring 3. Applications do not use POSIX sockets: they link libix.a and use either a low-level batched API (connect/accept/sendv/recv_done/close queued in a shared-memory array, results returned as knock/connected/recv/sent/dead event conditions) or ixev, a callback layer that 'behaves mostly like libevent'. Existing libevent servers must be ported; the memcached port changed about 150 lines of memcached.c.
how_it_is_fast: Each elastic thread runs to completion: it polls its own NIC RX ring, pushes a bounded batch (default 64 packets) through an lwIP-derived TCP/IP stack, switches to the application to consume events, then executes the application's batched system calls, TCP timers and TX in the same loop, with no interrupts and no intermediate socket buffers. Batching is adaptive, so batches only grow under congestion and light load keeps latency low. RSS flow-consistent hashing gives each hyperthread its own RX/TX queue pair, flows and memory pools, so the common path takes no locks and causes no cache-coherence traffic. The dataplane also uses only 2MB pages, a hierarchical timing wheel, and refills RX descriptors 32 at a time to cut PCIe writes.
when_to_use: Reproducing or extending the OSDI'14/SoCC'15 results: ix-project/ix-bench holds the memcached, ping-pong, short-message and connection-scaling scripts, and the ported memcached (ix branch of ix-project/memcached) and the mutilate load generator are public under ix-project.

Small-message TCP request/response servers (e.g. key-value GETs with <20B keys and 2B values) where p99 latency under a few hundred microseconds sets capacity, on a dedicated server with Intel 82599/X520/X540 10GbE.

High connection churn or many connections: the paper reports 3.8M TCP connections/s on 4x10GbE and runs up to 250K concurrent connections (at 250K, throughput falls to 47% of IX's peak from L3 cache misses).
Research on kernel-bypass designs that keep the network stack isolated from application code (VT-x ring separation) while Linux remains the control plane.
when_not_to_use: Anything production or long-lived: no commits since 2017-11-06, DPDK pinned at 16.04, and the maintainer said in 2021 (issue #36) that Dune has not been updated and likely does not support recent kernels.

Hardware or network setups outside its narrow support: non-Intel NICs (mlx4 was requested, never added, issue #24), machines without VT-x, non-x86, IPv6, SR-IOV, or more than one IX instance per host (issue #2).
Untrusted or bursty peers: libix has no receive flow control, and one flooding connection can terminate the server process (issue #12).
Applications that block in handlers or depend on POSIX sockets, TLS libraries or other socket-based code: every network path must be rewritten to ixev callbacks or the batched API.
Lock-heavy or CPU-bound servers: IX only removes kernel network overhead; memcached gained less on ETC (2.8x) and stopped scaling past 6 cores on IX because of its own lock contention.

integration.form: static lib (libix.a) linked into the application, which runs under the dp/ix dataplane binary; plus Linux kernel modules (dune.ko, pcidma.ko, igb_uio.ko) and a control-plane script
integration.dependencies: DPDK 16.04 (git submodule; ixgbe/i40e PMDs, eal, mbuf, mempool, ring), Dune (dune.ko + libdune, ix-project/dune has no license file), pcidma, igb_uio/uio, libconfig, libnuma, 2MB hugepages; cp/ixcp.py needs Python 2 and posix_ipc
integration.min_toolchain: Not documented. gcc builds the dataplane with -O3 -mno-red-zone -fno-pie; GCC 4.8 failed in DPDK's rte_memcpy.h when compiling i40e.c (issue #36; maintainer workaround: drop -no-pie from LDFLAGS and build with EXTRA_CFLAGS=-march=native). Control plane and ix-bench scripts are Python 2 only. Users report it running on Linux 3.16 and 4.4.
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux host with Intel VT-x; Intel 82599/X520/X540 NICs via ixgbe (README). An i40e (XL710) driver was added in 2016 but users report it receives and never transmits (issue #31, open). IPv4 only (ip_tuple holds 32-bit addresses).
integration.thread_safety: Per-thread design: each elastic thread owns its NIC queue, flow handles, memory pools and a __thread syscall batch array, so a handle is only used on the thread that owns it. The shared ARP table uses RCU. Elastic threads must not block; background threads may issue POSIX system calls, but the memcached port disabled its background maintenance threads with an 'XXX: hack' note that normal threads fail on newer kernels.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — ixev mimics libevent but supports only edge-triggered, persistent events with no event timeouts (ixev.h FIXME); applications must be ported off sockets/libevent, relinked against libix.a and launched as `dp/ix -- ./app`, and the NIC is unbound from Linux for IX's exclusive use

gotchas: No receive flow control: if one connection holds 128 unconsumed receive segments (IXEV_RECV_DEPTH), ixev prints 'ixev: ran out of receive memory' and calls exit(-1); a single `nc < /dev/zero` flood took down the echoserver (issue #12). A full syscall batch array likewise exits with 'ran out of command space'.

Zero-copy rules: received buffers are read-only and should be released quickly; send buffers must stay unmodified until the peer ACKs, or the wire payload is silently wrong. sendv returns bytes accepted by the TCP window, not bytes buffered, so partial sends are resumed on the 'sent' event.

The TCP stack runs on the application's threads: a slow handler stalls every flow hashed to that core, and IX flags the app non-responsive after about 10ms in user mode. Outbound connections pick ephemeral ports so RSS returns replies to the same thread, so two threads cannot share a flow.

Released artifacts differ from the paper: ix-bench's bench_memcached.py drives 2,720 connections from 16 threads (paper: 1,476), and the ported memcached disables its assoc-maintenance and slab-rebalance threads while the scripts pre-size the hash with hashpower=20. No IOMMU is used, so the dataplane is trusted with host-physical addresses; profiling needs `perf kvm --guest` because IX runs as a VT-x guest (issue #35).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick IX over mTCP or F-Stack only when you need the TCP stack protected from application code (separate rings under VT-x) or are reproducing the OSDI'14 comparison, where IX delivered 1.9x mTCP's short-message rate and lower 64B latency. Arrakis is the closer research analogue and adds IOMMU/SR-IOV support that IX lacks; for anything you must run today, F-Stack or Seastar are the maintained DPDK stacks.
verified_claims_summary: OSDI'14 paper: memcached-1.4.18 ported to libix on 6 cores vs. stock memcached (libevent+epoll) on 8 pinned, interrupt-tuned cores of Linux 3.16.1, on a Xeon E5-2665 @ 2.4 GHz server with Intel x520 (82599) 10GbE and 23 Linux mutilate clients over 1,476 connections. Max RPS within a 500us p99 SLA rose from 550K to 1,550K (ETC, 2.8x) and from 500K to 1,800K (USR, 3.6x), and unloaded p99 latency fell from 94 to 45us and from 85 to 32us; no compiler or version is given (the 2016 release builds the dataplane with gcc -O3).
status_note: Abandoned since 2017-11-06 (the maintainer still answered issues until 2021); IX's own code is MIT-style, but it needs the unlicensed Dune repo, kernel modules and DPDK 16.04 on old kernels, so treat it as a research artifact to study or reproduce, not a dependency.
